statement: Let $R \subseteq X \times Y$ be a [relation](c:relation) between finite sets. Let $K$ be the [simplicial complex](c:simplicial-complex) on $X$ whose simplices are the nonempty sets of $X$ with a common partner $y \in Y$, and let $L$ be the same complex on $Y$ for the transposed relation. Then $|K|$ and $|L|$ are [homotopy equivalent](c:homotopy-equivalence).

hypotheses.text: The set $R \subseteq X \times Y$ is a [relation](c:relation) between the sets $X$ and $Y$.
The sets $X$ and $Y$ are finite.

conclusion: The geometric realizations $|K|$ and $|L|$ are [homotopy equivalent](c:homotopy-equivalence).

proofs.name: Nerve theorem
proofs.slogan: Cover $K$ by the full simplices on the sets $R(y)$, identify the nerve of this cover with $L$, and apply the nerve theorem.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for finite $X$ and $Y$. A point without any related partner lies in neither complex and is ignored.

roles.why: The [relation](c:relation) defines the sets $A_y$ that cover $K$, and the same sets define the nerve $L$.
Finiteness makes every full simplex finite and the cover finite, so the nerve theorem applies to finite complexes.

steps.slogan: Cover $K$ by the full simplices on the sets $A_y$.
steps.detail: For $y \in Y$ let $A_y = \{x : x \mathrel{R} y\}$ and let $\Delta_y$ be the full [simplex](c:simplex) on $A_y$. Every subset of $A_y$ has the common partner $y$, so $\Delta_y \subseteq K$. Every simplex of $K$ has a common partner $y$, so it lies in $\Delta_y$. Hence $K = \bigcup_y \Delta_y$.

steps.slogan: Compute each finite intersection of the cover sets as a full simplex.
steps.detail: The intersection $\Delta_{y_0} \cap \dots \cap \Delta_{y_k}$ is the full simplex on $A_{y_0} \cap \dots \cap A_{y_k}$. This set is nonempty exactly when some $x$ is related to every $y_i$. A full simplex is [contractible](c:contractible-space), so every nonempty finite intersection is contractible.

steps.slogan: Identify the nerve of the cover with the complex $L$.
steps.detail: The nerve has one vertex $y$ for each nonempty $\Delta_y$, and $\{y_0, \dots, y_k\}$ is a simplex exactly when $\Delta_{y_0} \cap \dots \cap \Delta_{y_k} \neq \emptyset$. By step 2 this means that some $x$ is related to every $y_i$, which is the definition of $L$.

steps.slogan: Apply the nerve theorem to $K$ and its cover to get $|K| \simeq |L|$.
steps.detail: A [simplicial complex](c:simplicial-complex) covered by subcomplexes with contractible nonempty finite intersections is homotopy equivalent to the nerve of the cover. Steps 1 and 2 give the hypotheses, and step 3 shows that the nerve is $L$. So $|K|$ and $|L|$ are [homotopy equivalent](c:homotopy-equivalence).

concepts.c:relation: The relation supplies the sets $A_y$ for the cover and the transposed complex.
concepts.c:simplicial-complex: Both $K$ and $L$ are simplicial complexes, and $K$ is covered by subcomplexes.
concepts.c:homotopy-equivalence: The nerve theorem gives the homotopy equivalence between $|K|$ and the nerve.
concepts.c:simplex: Each cover set is a full simplex, which has a simple intersection pattern.
concepts.c:contractible-space: Contractible intersections are the hypothesis of the nerve theorem.

source.note: The nerve theorem proof of Dowker duality, as in Bjorner, Topological methods, Handbook of Combinatorics (1995), section 10.

proofs.name: Galois connection of face posets
proofs.slogan: Pass to the posets of simplices, match them by the two Galois-connected maps $N$ and $M$, and use that comparable maps are homotopic.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for finite $X$ and $Y$. The proof uses no nerve theorem and gives an explicit homotopy equivalence of the subdivisions.

roles.why: The [relation](c:relation) defines the maps $N$ and $M$ and the equivalence $\sigma \subseteq M(\tau) \iff \tau \subseteq N(\sigma)$.
Finiteness makes the sets $N(\sigma)$ and $M(\tau)$ finite, so they are simplices.

steps.slogan: Replace each complex by the poset of its simplices.
steps.detail: Let $F(K)$ be the poset of nonempty simplices of $K$ under inclusion, and define $F(L)$ in the same way. The order complex of $F(K)$ is the barycentric subdivision of $K$, so $|F(K)| \cong |K|$. Likewise $|F(L)| \cong |L|$, and the order complex of a poset equals that of its opposite.

steps.slogan: Define $N(\sigma)$ and $M(\tau)$ as the common partners of a simplex.
steps.detail: For $\sigma \in F(K)$ let $N(\sigma) = \{y : x \mathrel{R} y \text{ for all } x \in \sigma\}$. It is nonempty and finite, and any $x \in \sigma$ is a common partner of its subsets, so $N(\sigma) \in F(L)$. Define $M(\tau)$ symmetrically. Both maps reverse inclusion.

steps.slogan: Check that $\sigma \subseteq M(\tau)$ holds exactly when $\tau \subseteq N(\sigma)$.
steps.detail: Both conditions say that $x \mathrel{R} y$ for all $x \in \sigma$ and $y \in \tau$. Hence $\sigma \subseteq M(N(\sigma))$ and $\tau \subseteq N(M(\tau))$. The composite $M \circ N$ reverses inclusion twice, so it preserves it, and the same holds for $N \circ M$.

steps.slogan: Show that comparable order-preserving maps give homotopic maps of order complexes.
steps.detail: Let $\varphi \le \psi$ be order-preserving maps $P \to Q$. The map $P \times \{0 < 1\} \to Q$ that sends $(p,0)$ to $\varphi(p)$ and $(p,1)$ to $\psi(p)$ is order-preserving, and it gives a homotopy from $|\varphi|$ to $|\psi|$ on order complexes. So $|M \circ N| \simeq \mathrm{id}$ and $|N \circ M| \simeq \mathrm{id}$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $N$ and $M$ are inverse homotopy equivalences between the two order complexes.
steps.detail: The map $N$ is order-preserving from $F(K)$ to the opposite poset of $F(L)$, and $M$ goes back. By step 4 their composites are homotopic to the identity. So $|K| \cong |F(K)| \simeq |F(L)| \cong |L|$, which is a [homotopy equivalence](c:homotopy-equivalence).

concepts.c:relation: The relation defines both Galois-connected maps between the two posets.
concepts.c:simplicial-complex: The posets are the face posets of the two simplicial complexes.
concepts.c:homotopy-equivalence: The maps $N$ and $M$ give the homotopy equivalence of the theorem.

source.note: The Galois connection proof (Quillen's comparable-maps lemma applied to face posets), as in Bjorner, Topological methods, Handbook of Combinatorics (1995), section 10.

statement: Let $R \subseteq X \times Y$ be a [relation](c:relation) between sets. The [Vietoris complex](c:vietoris-complex) $V$ on $X$ has as simplices the finite nonempty sets with a common $R$-partner in $Y$. The [Čech nerve](c:cech-nerve) $C$ of the sets $\{x : x \mathrel{R} y\}$ is the same complex on $Y$. Then $V$ and $C$ have isomorphic [homology](c:homology) in every degree.

hypotheses.text: The set $R \subseteq X \times Y$ is a [relation](c:relation) between two arbitrary sets $X$ and $Y$.

proofs.name: Double complex of the relation
proofs.slogan: Build the double complex of pairs of tuples that are all related, and show that both projections are quasi-isomorphisms.
proofs.scope: Homology with integer coefficients, for sets of any size. The homotopy equivalence for finite sets is the member treated at the record Dowker duality.

roles.why: The [relation](c:relation) defines both complexes and the double complex $B_{p,q}$, and its symmetry exchanges the two projections.

steps.slogan: Form the double complex $B_{p,q}$ of pairs of related tuples.
steps.detail: Let $C_p(V)$ be the free abelian group on tuples $(x_0, \dots, x_p)$ with a common partner, with the alternating face boundary. It computes $H_*(V)$. Define $C_*(C)$ likewise on $Y$. Let $B_{p,q}$ be the free abelian group on pairs of tuples $(x_0..x_p; y_0..y_q)$ with $x_i \mathrel{R} y_j$ for all $i, j$, with boundaries $d'$ on the $x$-part and $d''$ on the $y$-part.

steps.slogan: Show that each column over a fixed $x$-tuple is acyclic.
steps.detail: Fix $a = (x_0, \dots, x_p)$ in $C_p(V)$ and let $N(a)$ be its nonempty set of common partners. The column over $a$ is the complex $\mathbb{Z}[N(a)^{q+1}]$. Pick $y^* \in N(a)$. Then $h(y_0, \dots, y_q) = (y^*, y_0, \dots, y_q)$ is a contracting homotopy of the augmented column, so its homology is $\mathbb{Z}$ in degree $0$ only.

steps.slogan: Deduce that the projection $\mathrm{Tot}\,B \to C_*(V)$ is a quasi-isomorphism.
steps.detail: The projection sends a pair $(a; y_0)$ to $a$ and the pairs with $q > 0$ to $0$. The columns have homology $\mathbb{Z}$ in degree $0$, so the standard spectral sequence of a first-quadrant [double complex](c:chain-complex) collapses. Hence the projection is an isomorphism on [homology](c:homology).

steps.slogan: Repeat the argument for rows to get $\mathrm{Tot}\,B \to C_*(C)$ as a quasi-isomorphism.
steps.detail: The definition of $B_{p,q}$ is symmetric in $x$ and $y$, because $R$ and its transpose define it in the same way. Steps 2 and 3 with the roles exchanged show that each row is acyclic and that the projection to $C_*(C)$ is a quasi-isomorphism.

steps.slogan: Compose the two quasi-isomorphisms to identify $H_n(V)$ with $H_n(C)$.
steps.detail: Both projections induce isomorphisms from $H_n(\mathrm{Tot}\,B)$. Therefore $H_n(V) \cong H_n(\mathrm{Tot}\,B) \cong H_n(C)$ for every $n \ge 0$.

concepts.c:relation: The relation defines both complexes and the symmetric double complex.
concepts.c:vietoris-complex: The Vietoris complex $V$ is one side of the isomorphism.
concepts.c:cech-nerve: The Čech nerve $C$ is the other side of the isomorphism.
concepts.c:homology: The proof compares the homology groups of the two complexes through a third complex.
concepts.c:chain-complex: The double complex is a family of chain complexes with a total complex.

source.note: The standard double complex argument for C. H. Dowker, Homology groups of relations, Annals of Mathematics 56 (1952), 84-95, which proves the theorem.

statement: Every finite simple [planar graph](c:planar-graph) has a proper vertex [colouring](c:graph-coloring) with at most five colours, so adjacent vertices get different colours.

hypotheses.text: The graph $G$ is a [planar graph](c:planar-graph), that is, it has a drawing in the plane without crossing edges.
The graph $G$ is finite and simple: it has no loops and no multiple edges.

conclusion: The vertices of $G$ can be coloured with colours $1, \dots, 5$ so that adjacent vertices have different colours.

proofs.name: Kempe chains
proofs.slogan: Remove a vertex of degree at most five, colour the rest by induction, and free a colour for it by swapping along a Kempe chain.
proofs.scope: Induction on the number of vertices, with at most five vertices as the base case. The map form follows by taking the dual graph, whose vertices are the regions of the map.

roles.why: Planarity gives Euler's formula and a vertex of small degree, keeps $G - v$ planar, and lets the Jordan curve theorem separate two neighbours.
Simplicity gives the edge bound $3n - 6$, and finiteness makes the induction on the vertex count work.

steps.slogan: Find a vertex of degree at most five by Euler's formula.
steps.detail: A simple [planar graph](c:planar-graph) with $n \ge 3$ vertices has at most $3n - 6$ edges, because every face has at least three edges and $V - E + F = 2$. The degree sum $2E \le 6n - 12$ is below $6n$, so some vertex $v$ has degree at most $5$.

steps.slogan: Delete the vertex $v$ and colour the smaller graph by induction.
steps.detail: The graph $G - v$ is simple and planar with fewer vertices. By the induction hypothesis it has a proper [colouring](c:graph-coloring) with colours $1, \dots, 5$. It remains to extend this colouring to $v$, after a recolouring if needed.

steps.slogan: Colour $v$ directly when its neighbours leave a colour unused.
steps.detail: If $v$ has at most four neighbours, or its neighbours use at most four colours, a free colour exists and the colouring extends. Otherwise $v$ has exactly five neighbours $v_1, \dots, v_5$, in this cyclic order around $v$ in the drawing, and they carry the colours $1, \dots, 5$.

steps.slogan: Swap colours 1 and 3 along the Kempe chain of $v_1$ if it misses $v_3$.
steps.detail: Let $K$ be the component of $v_1$ in the subgraph induced by the vertices of colour 1 or 3. This is a [Kempe chain](c:kempe-chain). If $v_3 \notin K$, exchange the two colours on $K$. The colouring stays proper, $v_1$ gets colour 3, no neighbour of $v$ has colour 1, and $v$ takes colour 1.

steps.slogan: Otherwise separate $v_2$ from $v_4$ by a closed curve and swap colours 2 and 4.
steps.detail: If $v_3 \in K$, a path of colours 1 and 3 from $v_1$ to $v_3$ together with $v$ forms a cycle. By the Jordan curve theorem it separates $v_2$ from $v_4$, so the 2-4 [Kempe chain](c:kempe-chain) of $v_2$ misses $v_4$. Swapping colours 2 and 4 on it frees colour 2 for $v$. Every case gives a proper 5-colouring.

concepts.c:planar-graph: Planarity gives a vertex of degree at most five and the separating cycle.
concepts.c:graph-coloring: The proof extends a proper colouring from $G - v$ to $G$.
concepts.c:kempe-chain: Swapping two colours along a Kempe chain keeps the colouring proper and frees a colour.

source.note: Heawood's 1890 proof (P. J. Heawood, Map-colour theorem, Quarterly Journal of Mathematics 24, 332-338), which repairs Kempe's argument; found in standard graph theory texts.

statement: Let $P$ be a [Sylow subgroup](c:sylow-subgroup) of a finite group $G$. Let the focal subgroup $P^*$ be generated by the commutators $[x, g] = x^{-1} g^{-1} x g$ with $x \in P$ and $g \in G$ that lie in $P$. Then $P \cap [G, G] = P^*$.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is a [finite group](c:finite-group).
The subgroup $P$ is a [Sylow](c:sylow-subgroup) $p$-subgroup of $G$ for a prime $p$.

conclusion: The intersection of $P$ with the [commutator subgroup](c:commutator-subgroup) $[G, G]$ equals the focal subgroup $P^*$.

formal.difference: The declaration assumes only that $P$ has finite index in $G$, so $G$ may be infinite. It states the same equality.

proofs.name: Transfer to $P/P^*$
proofs.slogan: Transfer $G$ into the abelian $p$-group $P/P^*$, where the transfer acts on $P$ as a power map prime to $p$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The inclusion $P^* \le P \cap [G,G]$ is direct, and the reverse inclusion uses the transfer.

roles.why: A [finite group](c:finite-group) has a Sylow subgroup of finite index, so the transfer exists and its power formula uses the index $[G:P]$.
The Sylow subgroup makes $P/P^*$ a $p$-group and makes the index $[G:P]$ prime to $p$.

steps.slogan: Show that the focal subgroup lies in $P$ and in the commutator subgroup.
steps.detail: Each generator $[x, g]$ is a commutator of $G$, so $P^* \le [G, G]$. Each generator lies in $P$ by definition, so $P^* \le P$. Hence $P^* \le P \cap [G, G]$.

steps.slogan: Form the abelian quotient $P/P^*$ that receives the transfer.
steps.detail: For $a, b \in P$ the commutator $[a, b]$ lies in $P$, so it is a generator of $P^*$. Hence $[P, P] \le P^*$ and $P/P^*$ is abelian. It is also a $p$-group, as a quotient of $P$.

steps.slogan: Define the [transfer homomorphism](c:transfer-homomorphism) $V \colon G \to P/P^*$ and kill $[G, G]$ with it.
steps.detail: Because $[G:P]$ is finite, the transfer into the abelian group $P/P^*$ is a homomorphism $V$. Its target is abelian, so $V$ is trivial on $[G, G]$. Hence $[G, G] \le \ker V$.

steps.slogan: Compute $V(x)$ for $x \in P$ as the power $x^{[G:P]}$ modulo $P^*$.
steps.detail: Let $\langle x \rangle$ act on the cosets $G/P$ by left multiplication. The transfer $V(x)$ is the product over the orbits of terms $g^{-1} x^m g$, where $m$ is the orbit size. Each term lies in $P$ and is congruent to $x^m$ modulo $P^*$. The orbit sizes sum to $[G:P]$, so $V(x) \equiv x^{[G:P]}$.

steps.slogan: Show $P \cap \ker V = P^*$ because the index $[G:P]$ is prime to $p$.
steps.detail: If $x \in P$ and $V(x) = 1$, then $x^{[G:P]} \in P^*$. In the $p$-group $P/P^*$ the power map by an integer prime to $p$ is injective, so $x \in P^*$. Thus $P \cap [G, G] \le P \cap \ker V \le P^* \le P \cap [G, G]$ by step 1.

concepts.c:finite-group: Finiteness gives a finite index and a well-defined transfer.
concepts.c:sylow-subgroup: The index of a Sylow subgroup is prime to $p$.
concepts.c:commutator-subgroup: The transfer kills the commutator subgroup, and the theorem identifies its part in $P$.
concepts.c:transfer-homomorphism: The transfer maps $G$ to $P/P^*$ and restricts to a power map on $P$.

source.note: mathlib uses focalSubgroup_le_commutator and focalSubgroup_le for one inclusion, and transferFocal_eq_pow with ker_transferFocal_inf_eq_focalSubgroup and Abelianization.commutator_subset_ker for the other.

statement: Every finite loopless [planar graph](c:planar-graph) has a proper vertex [colouring](c:colouring) with at most four colours. Equivalently, the regions of any map in the plane can be coloured with four colours so that regions that share a boundary segment get different colours.

hypotheses.text: The graph $G$ is a [planar graph](c:planar-graph).
The graph $G$ is finite and has no loops.

conclusion: The vertices of $G$ can be coloured with four colours so that adjacent vertices have different colours.

proofs.name: Discharging and reducible configurations
proofs.slogan: Take a minimal counterexample, show by discharging that it contains one of 633 configurations, and show by computer that each one is reducible.
proofs.scope: An outline of the 1997 proof of Robertson, Sanders, Seymour and Thomas. Steps 2 and 3 rest on computer checks that the cited papers describe and that this page does not reproduce.

roles.why: Planarity gives a triangulation by adding edges, and Euler's formula gives the total charge $12$ that discharging redistributes.
Finiteness allows a counterexample with the fewest vertices, and without loops a proper colouring can exist.

steps.slogan: Take a counterexample with the fewest vertices and make it a triangulation.
steps.detail: Suppose the theorem fails for some [planar graph](c:planar-graph) and pick a counterexample with the fewest vertices. Adding edges only restricts colourings, so it is a plane triangulation. The cited proof shows that it has minimum degree at least $5$ and no small separations except trivial ones, that is, it is internally 6-connected.

steps.slogan: Show by discharging that the triangulation contains one of 633 configurations.
steps.detail: Give each vertex the charge $6 - \deg v$. By Euler's formula the total charge is $12$. A set of 32 discharging rules moves charge between neighbours. If none of the 633 configurations occurred, all final charges would be at most $0$, which contradicts the total $12$.

steps.slogan: Verify by computer that each of the 633 configurations is reducible.
steps.detail: A [reducible configuration](c:reducible-configuration) cannot lie in a minimal counterexample. For each configuration, every 4-colouring of its boundary ring either extends to the interior directly or extends after a short sequence of Kempe chain switches. The authors check this by computer.

steps.slogan: Combine both lists to contradict the minimality of the counterexample.
steps.detail: By step 2 the minimal counterexample contains a configuration of the list. By step 3 a 4-[colouring](c:colouring) of the smaller graph obtained by deleting its interior extends to the configuration. This gives a 4-colouring of the counterexample, a contradiction.

concepts.c:planar-graph: Planarity gives the triangulation and the Euler charge count.
concepts.c:colouring: The proof extends a 4-colouring from a smaller graph to the whole graph.
concepts.c:reducible-configuration: Reducibility lets a colouring of a smaller graph extend across the configuration.

source.ref: N. Robertson, D. Sanders, P. Seymour and R. Thomas, The four-colour theorem, Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B 70 (1997), 2-44
source.note: A simplification of the first proof of K. Appel and W. Haken (Illinois Journal of Mathematics 21, 1977); G. Gonthier checked it in Coq.

statement: For a small [finitely complete](c:finitely-complete-category) category $C$, the category $\mathrm{Lex}(C, \mathrm{Set})$ of models of $C$, viewed as an [essentially algebraic theory](c:essentially-algebraic-theory), is [locally finitely presentable](c:locally-presentable-category), and $C \simeq (\mathrm{fp}\,\mathrm{Lex}(C, \mathrm{Set}))^{op}$. Every locally finitely presentable $K$ is $\mathrm{Lex}(C, \mathrm{Set})$ for $C = (\mathrm{fp}\,K)^{op}$, and $C \mapsto \mathrm{Lex}(C, \mathrm{Set})$ is a biequivalence.

hypotheses.text: The category $C$ is small.
The category $C$ has all finite limits, that is, it is [finitely complete](c:finitely-complete-category).

conclusion: The assignment $C \mapsto \mathrm{Lex}(C, \mathrm{Set})$ is a biequivalence from the opposite of the 2-category of small finitely complete categories and finite-limit-preserving functors to the 2-category of locally finitely presentable categories and finitary right adjoints.

proofs.name: Models as an Ind-completion
proofs.slogan: Show that $\mathrm{Lex}(C, \mathrm{Set})$ is the free filtered-colimit completion of $C^{op}$, read off $C$ from its finitely presentable objects, and match the morphisms.
proofs.scope: An outline of the proof of Gabriel and Ulmer in the form given by Adámek and Rosický. The 2-categorical bookkeeping (2-cells) is cited, not written out.

roles.why: Smallness makes $\mathrm{Lex}(C, \mathrm{Set})$ a locally small category and makes $\mathrm{fp}\,K$ a small category.
Finite limits make elements of a lex functor cofiltered and make every idempotent of $C$ split.

steps.slogan: Show that $\mathrm{Lex}(C, \mathrm{Set})$ is the free filtered-colimit completion of $C^{op}$.
steps.detail: A functor $F \colon C \to \mathrm{Set}$ preserves finite limits exactly when its category of elements is cofiltered. Then $F$ is the filtered colimit of the representables $C(c, -)$ over its elements. Representables are finitely presentable, so $\mathrm{Lex}(C, \mathrm{Set}) \simeq \mathrm{Ind}(C^{op})$, which is [locally finitely presentable](c:locally-presentable-category).

steps.slogan: Recover $C$ as the opposite of the finitely presentable objects.
steps.detail: The finitely presentable objects of $\mathrm{Ind}(D)$ are the retracts of objects of $D$. A category with equalizers splits its idempotents, because $e$ splits through the equalizer of $e$ and the identity. So $\mathrm{fp}\,\mathrm{Lex}(C, \mathrm{Set}) \simeq C^{op}$.

steps.slogan: Show that every locally finitely presentable category $K$ has this form.
steps.detail: In $K$ the full subcategory $\mathrm{fp}\,K$ is small and has finite colimits, and $K \simeq \mathrm{Ind}(\mathrm{fp}\,K)$. Put $C = (\mathrm{fp}\,K)^{op}$; it has finite limits. By step 1, $K \simeq \mathrm{Lex}(C, \mathrm{Set})$.

steps.slogan: Match finite-limit-preserving functors with finitary right adjoints.
steps.detail: A lex functor $F \colon C \to D$ gives the precomposition $\mathrm{Lex}(D, \mathrm{Set}) \to \mathrm{Lex}(C, \mathrm{Set})$. It preserves limits and filtered colimits and has a left adjoint, left Kan extension along $F$. Conversely a finitary right adjoint has a left adjoint that keeps finitely presentable objects, and this restricts to a lex functor.

steps.slogan: Assemble steps 1 to 4 into a biequivalence of 2-categories.
steps.detail: Steps 1 and 3 show that the assignment hits every locally finitely presentable category up to equivalence. Steps 2 and 4 show that it is full and faithful on functors, and natural transformations correspond in the same way. Hence $C \mapsto \mathrm{Lex}(C, \mathrm{Set})$ is a biequivalence.

concepts.c:finitely-complete-category: Finite limits make the elements of a lex functor cofiltered.
concepts.c:essentially-algebraic-theory: A small finitely complete category is an essentially algebraic theory, and its models are lex functors.
concepts.c:locally-presentable-category: Locally finitely presentable categories are exactly the model categories of such theories.

source.ref: J. Adámek and J. Rosický, Locally Presentable and Accessible Categories, London Mathematical Society Lecture Note Series 189, Cambridge University Press, 1994, Chapter 1; after P. Gabriel and F. Ulmer, Lokal präsentierbare Kategorien, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 221, Springer, 1971
source.note: The original theorem is in Gabriel and Ulmer; Adámek and Rosický give the modern proof through Ind-completions.

statement: Let $k$ be a perfect field of characteristic $p$ and $\Gamma$ a [formal group](c:formal-group) of finite height $n$ over $k$. The [Morava E-theory](c:morava-e-theory) spectrum $E(k, \Gamma)$ of the [Lubin-Tate](c:lubin-tate-theory) universal deformation has an essentially unique [E-infinity ring](c:e-infinity-ring) structure. The assignment $(k, \Gamma) \mapsto E(k, \Gamma)$ is functorial, so $\mathrm{Aut}(k, \Gamma)$ acts by $E_\infty$ ring maps.

hypotheses.text: The field $k$ is perfect of characteristic $p > 0$.
The [formal group](c:formal-group) $\Gamma$ over $k$ has finite height $n \ge 1$.

conclusion: The spectrum $E(k, \Gamma)$ has an essentially unique $E_\infty$ ring structure that depends functorially on $(k, \Gamma)$, and $\mathrm{Aut}(k, \Gamma)$ acts on it by $E_\infty$ ring maps.

proofs.name: Goerss-Hopkins obstruction theory
proofs.slogan: Build the Lubin-Tate spectrum, set up the moduli space of $E_\infty$ structures as a tower, and show that its obstruction groups vanish.
proofs.scope: An outline of the Goerss-Hopkins proof for the pairs $(k, \Gamma)$ of the statement. The vanishing computations are cited, not written out.

roles.why: A perfect field of characteristic $p$ carries the Witt vectors $W(k)$ that form the base of the Lubin-Tate ring.
Finite height makes the deformation space a power series ring, whose cohomology the proof computes.

steps.slogan: Form the Lubin-Tate ring and the Landweber exact spectrum $E(k, \Gamma)$.
steps.detail: Lubin-Tate theory gives the universal deformation of $\Gamma$ over $W(k)[[u_1, \dots, u_{n-1}]]$. The Landweber exact functor theorem then gives an even periodic, homotopy commutative ring spectrum $E(k, \Gamma)$ with this formal group, and the construction is functorial in the pair on homotopy ring spectra.

steps.slogan: Express the space of $E_\infty$ structures as a tower with André-Quillen layers.
steps.detail: Goerss and Hopkins study the space of $E_\infty$ ring spectra $X$ with a given $E_*X$ as a comodule algebra. They write it as the limit of a tower of spaces. The layers and obstructions to lifting through the tower lie in [André-Quillen](c:andre-quillen-homology) cohomology groups of that algebra.

steps.slogan: Prove that the obstruction groups for $E(k, \Gamma)$ vanish.
steps.detail: For the comodule algebra of $E(k, \Gamma)$ the relevant André-Quillen cohomology groups are computed with the help of Lubin-Tate deformation theory, and they vanish in the degrees that matter. So every obstruction is zero and the layers of the tower are trivial.

steps.slogan: Conclude that an $E_\infty$ structure exists and is essentially unique.
steps.detail: With the obstruction groups zero, the tower has a lift at each stage and the choices are trivial. Hence $E(k, \Gamma)$ has an $E_\infty$ ring structure that realizes the given algebra data, and any two such structures agree up to the contractible choices of the tower.

steps.slogan: Apply the same vanishing to mapping spaces to make the construction functorial.
steps.detail: The space of $E_\infty$ maps $E(k, \Gamma) \to E(k', \Gamma')$ is computed by a similar tower with the same vanishing groups, so it is homotopy discrete, with components the maps of pairs. This lifts the functor to $E_\infty$ rings, and $\mathrm{Aut}(k, \Gamma)$ acts on $E(k, \Gamma)$ by $E_\infty$ maps.

concepts.c:formal-group: The formal group of finite height is the input of Lubin-Tate theory.
concepts.c:morava-e-theory: Morava E-theory is the spectrum that receives the structured ring structure.
concepts.c:lubin-tate-theory: Lubin-Tate theory gives the deformation ring and the group action on it.
concepts.c:e-infinity-ring: An $E_\infty$ ring structure is the extra structure that the theorem constructs.
concepts.c:andre-quillen-homology: André-Quillen cohomology holds the obstructions in the moduli tower.

source.ref: P. G. Goerss and M. J. Hopkins, Moduli spaces of commutative ring spectra, in: Structured Ring Spectra, London Mathematical Society Lecture Note Series 315, Cambridge University Press, 2004, 151-200
source.note: The last section applies the obstruction theory to the Lubin-Tate spectra; the theorem also carries the name of H. Miller and J. Lurie.

statement: For every finite graph $H$ there is $k$ such that every finite graph with no $H$ [minor](c:graph-minor) has a tree decomposition of adhesion at most $k$ whose torsos are $k$-nearly embeddable: after deleting at most $k$ vertices, a torso embeds in a [surface](c:surface-embedding) of Euler genus at most $k$, with at most $k$ vortices of width at most $k$.

hypotheses.text: The graph $H$ is a fixed finite graph.
The finite graph $G$ has no [minor](c:graph-minor) isomorphic to $H$.

conclusion: The graph $G$ has a tree decomposition of adhesion at most $k = k(H)$ in which every torso is $k$-nearly embeddable in a surface of Euler genus at most $k$.

proofs.name: Tangles, flat walls and vortices
proofs.slogan: Split $G$ along small separations to isolate its large tangles, then near-embed the part that each tangle controls.
proofs.scope: An outline of the Robertson-Seymour proof; the planar $H$ is the easy case, and the case of a non-planar $H$ rests on the cited papers. The statement is also available in the improved form of Diestel, Kawarabayashi, Müller and Wollan.

roles.why: The size and planarity of $H$ fix the constant $k$ and decide between the bounded-treewidth case and the surface case.
Excluding a [minor](c:graph-minor) bounds the treewidth in the planar case and makes large walls flat in the other case.

steps.slogan: Settle the case of planar $H$ by the grid theorem.
steps.detail: If $H$ is planar, a graph with no $H$ [minor](c:graph-minor) has bounded [treewidth](c:treewidth), by the grid theorem of Robertson and Seymour. The trivial tree decomposition has bags of bounded size, and each torso is nearly embeddable by deleting all its vertices as apices.

steps.slogan: Separate the large tangles of $G$ by a tree decomposition of small adhesion.
steps.detail: For non-planar $H$, the tangle tree-decomposition theorem gives a tree decomposition of bounded adhesion in which each large tangle of $G$ is controlled by one bag and distinct large tangles lie in different bags. Bags with no large tangle have bounded treewidth.

steps.slogan: Find a large wall in each tangle and make it flat after deleting few vertices.
steps.detail: A large tangle controls a large wall. Because $G$ has no $H$ minor, it has no large complete minor, and the flat wall theorem gives a set of at most $a(H)$ apex vertices after whose deletion the wall is flat, that is, drawn in a plane region.

steps.slogan: Draw the controlled part on a surface of bounded genus with bounded vortices.
steps.detail: Robertson and Seymour show that, after deleting apices, the part controlled by the tangle embeds in a [surface](c:surface-embedding) except for vortices of bounded width in some faces. Each handle or crosscap added to reach the embedding makes $H$ harder to embed, so the Euler genus is bounded in terms of $H$.

steps.slogan: Assemble the tree decomposition with nearly embeddable torsos.
steps.detail: Combine the tree decomposition of step 2 with the near-embeddings of step 4 in the bags that carry a tangle, and with the bounded bags elsewhere. Taking $k$ as the largest of the constants gives adhesion at most $k$ and $k$-nearly embeddable torsos.

concepts.c:graph-minor: The excluded minor drives every step: bounded treewidth, flat walls and genus bounds.
concepts.c:surface-embedding: Each torso is nearly embedded in a surface of bounded Euler genus.
concepts.c:treewidth: In the planar case the excluded minor bounds the treewidth.

source.ref: N. Robertson and P. D. Seymour, Graph Minors. XVI. Excluding a non-planar graph, Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B 89 (2003), 43-76
source.note: With the earlier papers of the series (grid theorem in V, tangle trees in X, vortices in XVII); see also R. Diestel, K. Kawarabayashi, T. Müller and P. Wollan, JCTB 102 (2012), 1189-1210.

statement: A [finitely generated group](c:finitely-generated-group) has polynomial [growth](c:word-growth) if and only if it has a [nilpotent subgroup](c:nilpotent-group) of finite index.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is a [finitely generated group](c:finitely-generated-group), with word metric from a finite generating set.

conclusion: The ball $B(n)$ of radius $n$ has at most $C n^d$ elements for some $C$ and $d$ exactly when $G$ has a nilpotent subgroup of finite index.

proofs.name: Gromov: limit spaces and Lie groups
proofs.slogan: Rescale the Cayley graph, take a Gromov-Hausdorff limit, use the structure theory of locally compact groups, and induct on the growth degree.
proofs.scope: An outline of Gromov's proof of the hard direction; the converse direction is the classical estimate of Wolf and Bass. Steps 2 to 4 rest on the cited paper and on the solution of Hilbert's fifth problem.

roles.why: Finite generation gives the [Cayley graph](c:cayley-graph), its rescalings and a growth function that is finite at every radius.

steps.slogan: Show that a group with a nilpotent subgroup of finite index has polynomial growth.
steps.detail: A finite-index subgroup of a finitely generated group has the same growth type. A finitely generated [nilpotent group](c:nilpotent-group) has a central series with finitely generated abelian factors, and Wolf and Bass bound the ball size by a polynomial of degree $\sum_k k \cdot \mathrm{rank}(\gamma_k/\gamma_{k+1})$.

steps.slogan: Rescale the Cayley graph at doubling scales and extract a limit space.
steps.detail: If $|B(n)| \le C n^d$, there are radii $R_i \to \infty$ with $|B(2R_i)| \le C' |B(R_i)|$. The rescaled [Cayley graphs](c:cayley-graph) $(G, d/R_i)$ are uniformly doubling, so a subsequence has a [Gromov-Hausdorff limit](c:gromov-hausdorff-convergence) $Y$ that is locally compact, connected and finite dimensional.

steps.slogan: Build a Lie group from the isometries of the limit space.
steps.detail: Gromov builds from the isometries of the rescaled spaces a locally compact group that acts transitively on $Y$. Because $Y$ is finite dimensional, the solution of Hilbert's fifth problem by Montgomery and Zippin makes this group a [Lie group](c:lie-group) up to a compact factor. For infinite $G$ this gives a homomorphism to a Lie group with infinite image.

steps.slogan: Pass to a finite-index subgroup that maps onto $\mathbb{Z}$.
steps.detail: The image is a finitely generated linear group of polynomial growth, and such a group is virtually nilpotent by the appendix of Tits. An infinite virtually nilpotent group has a nilpotent subgroup of finite index with infinite abelianization. Pulling back gives a finite-index subgroup $G_0 \le G$ with a map onto $\mathbb{Z}$.

steps.slogan: Induct on the growth degree through the kernel of the map onto $\mathbb{Z}$.
steps.detail: The kernel $N$ of $G_0 \to \mathbb{Z}$ is finitely generated and has polynomial growth of smaller degree than $G_0$. By induction $N$ is virtually nilpotent, so $G_0$ is virtually polycyclic, and Wolf's theorem makes a polycyclic group of polynomial growth virtually nilpotent. A finite group is the base case.

steps.slogan: Combine the two directions into the equivalence.
steps.detail: Step 1 shows that a group with a nilpotent subgroup of finite index has polynomial growth. Steps 2 to 5 show that an infinite group of polynomial growth has a nilpotent subgroup of finite index, and a finite group has one trivially.

concepts.c:finitely-generated-group: Finite generation defines the word metric and the growth function.
concepts.c:word-growth: Polynomial growth is the hypothesis that makes the rescaled spaces doubling.
concepts.c:nilpotent-group: Nilpotent groups are the target class, and their growth is polynomial.
concepts.c:cayley-graph: The Cayley graph is the metric space whose large-scale shape the proof studies.
concepts.c:gromov-hausdorff-convergence: The limit of the rescaled graphs carries the isometric group action.
concepts.c:lie-group: The isometry group of the limit is a Lie group, which gives a map onto $\mathbb{Z}$.

source.ref: M. Gromov, Groups of polynomial growth and expanding maps (with an appendix by J. Tits), Publications Mathématiques de l'IHÉS 53 (1981), 53-78
source.note: The easy direction is due to J. A. Wolf (1968) and H. Bass (1972).

proofs.name: Kleiner: harmonic functions
proofs.slogan: Use the finite dimension of the space of harmonic functions of polynomial growth to get a finite-index subgroup that maps onto the integers, then induct.
proofs.scope: An outline of Kleiner's proof of the hard direction; it avoids the structure theory of locally compact groups. The converse direction is the same estimate as in the first proof.

roles.why: Finite generation gives the Cayley graph, its Laplacian and the translation action of $G$ on harmonic functions.

steps.slogan: Check doubling and a Poincaré inequality on the Cayley graph.
steps.detail: Polynomial [growth](c:word-growth) gives the doubling property of balls at infinitely many scales. The [Cayley graph](c:cayley-graph) of any finitely generated group satisfies a scale-invariant Poincaré inequality, so the analysis of the next step applies.

steps.slogan: Show that harmonic functions of polynomial growth form a finite-dimensional space.
steps.detail: Following Colding and Minicozzi, Kleiner uses doubling and the Poincaré inequality to show that, for each $d$, the space of [harmonic functions](c:harmonic-function) on the Cayley graph of growth at most $d$ has finite dimension.

steps.slogan: Let $G$ act by translation on the harmonic functions modulo constants.
steps.detail: For infinite $G$ Kleiner finds a nonconstant harmonic function $u$ of polynomial growth. The group $G$ acts by translation on the finite-dimensional space of such functions modulo constants. This gives a finite-dimensional linear representation of $G$ that is not trivial.

steps.slogan: Obtain a finite-index subgroup with a map onto $\mathbb{Z}$ from this representation.
steps.detail: If the image is finite, its kernel $K$ has finite index and $u(gx) - u(x) = c(g)$ for $g \in K$. The maximum principle on the finite quotient shows that the homomorphism $c \colon K \to \mathbb{R}$ is nonzero. If the image is infinite, it is a linear group of polynomial growth, hence virtually nilpotent. Either way a finite-index subgroup maps onto $\mathbb{Z}$.

steps.slogan: Induct on the growth degree through the kernel of the map onto $\mathbb{Z}$.
steps.detail: The kernel is finitely generated and its growth degree is smaller. By induction it is virtually nilpotent, so the finite-index subgroup is virtually polycyclic, and Wolf's theorem gives a nilpotent subgroup of finite index in $G$. A finite group is the base case.

steps.slogan: Combine this direction with the polynomial estimate for nilpotent groups.
steps.detail: The estimate of Wolf and Bass shows that a group with a nilpotent subgroup of finite index has polynomial growth. Steps 1 to 5 show the converse for infinite groups, and a finite group has such a subgroup trivially.

concepts.c:finitely-generated-group: Finite generation gives the Cayley graph and the translation action on harmonic functions.
concepts.c:word-growth: Polynomial growth gives doubling at infinitely many scales.
concepts.c:nilpotent-group: Nilpotent groups are the target class, and their growth is polynomial.
concepts.c:cayley-graph: The harmonic functions live on the Cayley graph.
concepts.c:harmonic-function: Harmonic functions of polynomial growth carry the representation of the group.

source.ref: B. Kleiner, A new proof of Gromov's theorem on groups of polynomial growth, Journal of the American Mathematical Society 23 (2010), 815-829
source.note: The finite-dimensionality argument builds on T. H. Colding and W. P. Minicozzi II.

statement: Let $M$ be a homotopy commutative [topological monoid](c:topological-monoid). The map $M \to \Omega BM$ into the [loop space](c:loop-space) of the [classifying space](c:classifying-space) induces an isomorphism of [Pontryagin rings](c:pontrjagin-ring) $H_*(M)[\pi_0(M)^{-1}] \cong H_*(\Omega BM)$, where the left side is the [localization](c:localization-of-a-ring) at the components.

hypotheses.text: The space $M$ is a [topological monoid](c:topological-monoid) whose unit is a nondegenerate basepoint.
The multiplication of $M$ is homotopy commutative: $xy$ and $yx$ are homotopic as maps $M \times M \to M$.

conclusion: The map $M \to \Omega BM$ induces a ring isomorphism $H_*(M)[\pi_0(M)^{-1}] \to H_*(\Omega BM)$.

proofs.name: Telescope and homology fibration
proofs.slogan: Invert the components by a telescope, and show that the telescope is the homotopy fibre of a contractible space over $BM$ by a homology fibration.
proofs.scope: The theorem for homology with integer coefficients. The criterion that identifies a homology fibration is the cited step; the rest is written out.

roles.why: The monoid acts on itself and on the telescope, and it has a [bar construction](c:bar-construction) and a classifying space $BM$.
Homotopy commutativity makes the component classes central in $H_*(M)$, so the colimit is the localization and each component acts invertibly.

steps.slogan: Form the telescope $M_\infty$ of right multiplications by representatives of all components.
steps.detail: Choose points $m_1, m_2, \dots$ of $M$ so that every component divides some product $m_1 \cdots m_k$ up to homotopy. Let $M_\infty$ be the [mapping telescope](c:mapping-telescope) of $M \xrightarrow{\cdot m_1} M \xrightarrow{\cdot m_2} \cdots$. It is a left $M$-space, and $H_*(M_\infty) = \mathrm{colim}\, H_*(M) = H_*(M)[\pi_0(M)^{-1}]$ because the classes $[m_i]$ are central.

steps.slogan: Show that every element of $M$ acts on $M_\infty$ by a homology equivalence.
steps.detail: Left multiplication by $g \in M$ acts on $H_*(M_\infty)$ as multiplication by $[g]$. The classes $[m_i]$ are cofinal and central, so $[g]$ divides a product $[m_1 \cdots m_k]$ that is a unit in the localization. Hence $[g]$ is invertible and left translation is a homology isomorphism.

steps.slogan: Apply the homology fibration criterion to $B(*, M, M_\infty) \to BM$.
steps.detail: McDuff and Segal prove that if $M$ acts on $X$ and every translation $x \mapsto mx$ is a homology equivalence, then $B(*, M, X) \to BM$ is a homology fibration with fibre $X$. Step 2 gives the hypothesis for $X = M_\infty$.

steps.slogan: Show that $B(*, M, M_\infty)$ is contractible.
steps.detail: The [bar construction](c:bar-construction) $B(*, M, M)$ is contractible, and $B$ commutes with the telescope: $B(*, M, M_\infty)$ is the telescope of copies of $B(*, M, M)$. A telescope of contractible spaces is contractible.

steps.slogan: Compare the fibre with the loop space to get $H_*(M_\infty) \cong H_*(\Omega BM)$.
steps.detail: Because $B(*, M, M_\infty)$ is contractible, the homotopy fibre of its map to $BM$ is $\Omega BM$. For a homology fibration the inclusion of the fibre $M_\infty$ into the homotopy fibre is a homology equivalence. This map extends $M \to \Omega BM$, so $H_*(M)[\pi_0(M)^{-1}] \cong H_*(\Omega BM)$ as rings.

concepts.c:topological-monoid: The monoid $M$ acts on itself and has a bar construction.
concepts.c:loop-space: The loop space $\Omega BM$ is the homotopy fibre that the proof identifies.
concepts.c:classifying-space: The classifying space $BM$ is the base of the homology fibration.
concepts.c:pontrjagin-ring: The multiplication of $M$ makes $H_*(M)$ a ring, and the isomorphism respects it.
concepts.c:localization-of-a-ring: Inverting the component classes is the algebraic side of the theorem.
concepts.c:bar-construction: The bar construction builds $BM$ and the contractible total space.
concepts.c:mapping-telescope: The telescope inverts the component classes in homology.

source.ref: D. McDuff and G. Segal, Homology fibrations and the group-completion theorem, Inventiones Mathematicae 31 (1976), 279-284
source.note: Their Proposition 2 is the homology fibration criterion of step 3.

statement: Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be an interval and let $f_n \colon I \to \mathbb{R}$ be [monotone functions](c:monotone-function) with $|f_n(x)| \le M$ for all $n$ and $x$. Then some [subsequence](c:subsequence) of $(f_n)$ converges at every point of $I$.

hypotheses.text: The domain $I$ is an interval of real numbers.
Each $f_n$ is a [monotone function](c:monotone-function), increasing or decreasing.
The functions are uniformly bounded: $|f_n(x)| \le M$ for all $n$ and all $x \in I$.

conclusion: A subsequence $(f_{n_k})$ converges at every $x \in I$, and its limit is a monotone function.

proofs.name: Two diagonal arguments
proofs.slogan: Extract a subsequence that converges on a countable dense set, show that monotonicity gives convergence off a countable set, and extract again on that set.
proofs.scope: The statement for monotone functions on any interval. The version for functions of uniformly bounded [variation](c:bounded-variation) follows by writing each function as a difference of two uniformly bounded monotone functions.

roles.why: The interval has a countable dense subset and a linear order for the squeeze.
Monotonicity gives the squeeze between rational values and bounds the number of jumps.
The uniform bound gives convergent subsequences at each fixed point.

steps.slogan: Pass to a subsequence of functions that all increase.
steps.detail: Infinitely many $f_n$ are increasing, or infinitely many are decreasing. Keep that subsequence and replace $f_n$ by $-f_n$ in the second case. The bound $M$ stays, and a limit of $-f_n$ gives a limit of $f_n$.

steps.slogan: Extract a subsequence that converges at every point of a countable dense set.
steps.detail: Let $D \subseteq I$ be a [countable](c:countable-set) [dense](c:dense-set) set that contains the endpoints lying in $I$, and list it as $q_1, q_2, \dots$. By the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem, refine the sequence so that it converges at $q_1$, then at $q_2$, and so on. The diagonal sequence $g_k$ converges at every $q \in D$ to some $g(q)$, and $g$ is increasing on $D$.

steps.slogan: Squeeze $g_k(x)$ between the limits at points of $D$ on both sides of $x$.
steps.detail: Put $\ell(x) = \sup\{g(q) : q \in D, q < x\}$ and $u(x) = \inf\{g(r) : r \in D, r > x\}$. For $q < x < r$ in $D$ we have $g_k(q) \le g_k(x) \le g_k(r)$, so $\ell(x) \le \liminf g_k(x) \le \limsup g_k(x) \le u(x)$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\ell(x) = u(x)$ except at countably many points.
steps.detail: For $x < y$ choose $r \in D$ with $x < r < y$. Then $u(x) \le g(r) \le \ell(y)$, so the open intervals $(\ell(x), u(x))$ with $\ell(x) < u(x)$ are pairwise disjoint and each holds a rational. Hence the set $E$ of such $x$, together with the endpoints, is countable. On $I \setminus E$ the sequence $g_k(x)$ converges.

steps.slogan: Extract a further subsequence that converges at every point of $E$.
steps.detail: The set $E$ is countable and each $g_k(x)$ is bounded, so the diagonal argument of step 2 gives a subsequence that converges on $E$. It still converges on $I \setminus E$, as a subsequence of a convergent sequence. It converges at every point of $I$, and the limit is increasing as a pointwise limit of increasing functions.

concepts.c:monotone-function: Monotonicity gives the squeeze and the countable set of jumps.
concepts.c:subsequence: The theorem asserts a convergent subsequence, built by two extractions.
concepts.c:bounded-variation: Bounded variation reduces to the monotone case by the Jordan decomposition.
concepts.c:countable-set: A countable set allows the diagonal extraction of one subsequence.
concepts.c:dense-set: A dense countable set controls the values of monotone functions between its points.

source.note: The classical diagonal argument over the rationals followed by a second diagonal argument over the countably many jumps of the limit.

statement: Let $X_*$ be a filtered space, and let $X$ be the union of the interiors of subsets $U^\lambda$, with $U^\lambda_i = U^\lambda \cap X_i$. If all finite intersections of the filtered spaces $U^\lambda_*$ are connected, then $X_*$ is connected, and the fundamental [crossed complex](c:crossed-complex) $\Pi$ turns the [coequalizer](c:coequalizer) $\coprod U^{\lambda\mu}_* \rightrightarrows \coprod U^\lambda_* \to X_*$ into a coequalizer of crossed complexes.

hypotheses.text: The space $X_*$ is a filtered space $X_0 \subseteq X_1 \subseteq \dots \subseteq X$.
The space $X$ is the union of the interiors of subsets $U^\lambda$, and $U^\lambda_i = U^\lambda \cap X_i$.
Every finite intersection of the filtered spaces $U^\lambda_*$ is a [connected filtered space](c:connected-filtered-space).

conclusion: The filtered space $X_*$ is connected, and $\Pi X_*$ is the coequalizer of $\coprod \Pi U^{\lambda\mu}_* \rightrightarrows \coprod \Pi U^\lambda_*$ in crossed complexes.

proofs.name: Algebraic inverse to subdivision
proofs.slogan: Model the crossed complex by filtered cubes, subdivide each cube into small cubes inside the cover, and compose them back algebraically.
proofs.scope: The crossed complex form of Brown and Higgins; in dimension 2 it gives the pushout theorem for [crossed modules](c:crossed-module), and the [homotopy colimit](c:homotopy-colimit) form is the member treated at the record higher van Kampen theorem. The proof is an outline that cites the cubical machinery.

roles.why: The filtration defines the filtered cubes and the crossed complex $\Pi X_*$.
The interiors cover $X$, so the Lebesgue lemma subdivides every cube into cubes that lie in single sets $U^\lambda$.
[Connectedness](c:connected-filtered-space) lets the small cubes be deformed to cubes with vertices in $X_0$ that compose.

steps.slogan: Describe $\Pi X_*$ by filtered cubes up to filtered homotopy.
steps.detail: Let $\rho_n X_*$ be the set of filtered maps $I^n_* \to X_*$ modulo filtered homotopy rel vertices. These sets have compositions in $n$ directions and form a cubical $\omega$-groupoid with connections $\rho X_*$.

steps.slogan: Reduce the claim to cubical $\omega$-groupoids by the equivalence with crossed complexes.
steps.detail: Brown and Higgins prove that the category of crossed complexes is equivalent to the category of $\omega$-groupoids with connections, and that $\rho X_*$ corresponds to $\Pi X_*$. So it is enough to show that $\rho$ preserves the coequalizer.

steps.slogan: Subdivide each cube so that every small cube lies in one set $U^\lambda$.
steps.detail: Take a filtered cube $I^n_* \to X_*$. The preimages of the interiors of the $U^\lambda$ cover the compact cube, so the Lebesgue number lemma gives a subdivision whose small cubes each map into one $U^\lambda$.

steps.slogan: Use connectedness to deform the small cubes into composable cubes of the pieces.
steps.detail: The connectivity conditions say that every component of $X_i$ meets $X_0$ and that $\pi_j(X_i, X_{i-1}, v) = 0$ for $1 \le j < i$. They let Brown and Higgins deform the subdivided cube, so that its small cubes have vertices in $X_0$ and lie in the sets $\rho U^\lambda_*$. The cube is then a composite of such cubes.

steps.slogan: Check the universal property of the coequalizer for $\rho X_*$ and conclude.
steps.detail: Step 4 shows that $\coprod \rho U^\lambda_* \to \rho X_*$ is surjective on cubes. Two subdivisions have a common refinement, and the composite of a subdivided cube does not depend on the choice, which gives injectivity modulo the relations from $U^{\lambda\mu}$. Hence $\rho X_*$, and so $\Pi X_*$, is the coequalizer. Connectedness of $X_*$ follows from the same deformations.

concepts.c:crossed-complex: The crossed complex is the algebraic invariant that the theorem computes as a colimit.
concepts.c:coequalizer: The theorem says that the invariant turns a coequalizer of spaces into a coequalizer.
concepts.c:connected-filtered-space: Connectedness makes subdivided cubes deformable into composable cubes.
concepts.c:crossed-module: In dimension 2 the crossed complex gives a crossed module of relative homotopy groups.
concepts.c:homotopy-colimit: The homotopy colimit form is the companion statement for the homotopy type.

source.ref: R. Brown and P. J. Higgins, Colimit theorems for relative homotopy groups, Journal of Pure and Applied Algebra 22 (1981), 11-41; see also R. Brown, P. J. Higgins and R. Sivera, Nonabelian Algebraic Topology, EMS Tracts in Mathematics 15, European Mathematical Society, 2011
source.note: The slogan of the proof is 'algebraic inverses to subdivision'.

statement: Let $X$ be a space with an [open cover](c:open-cover) $\{U_\lambda\}$ that has a locally finite subordinate partition of unity, for example $X$ paracompact. Then the projection from the [homotopy colimit](c:homotopy-colimit) of the finite intersections $U_{\lambda_0} \cap \dots \cap U_{\lambda_k}$ to $X$ is a [homotopy equivalence](c:homotopy-equivalence).

hypotheses.text: The family $\{U_\lambda\}$ is an [open cover](c:open-cover) of the space $X$.
There is a locally finite partition of unity $\{\varphi_\lambda\}$ with $\mathrm{supp}\,\varphi_\lambda \subseteq U_\lambda$.

conclusion: The projection $p \colon E \to X$ from the homotopy colimit $E$ of the Čech diagram is a homotopy equivalence, so $X$ is the homotopy colimit of the pieces and their overlaps.

proofs.name: Partition of unity section
proofs.slogan: Use the partition of unity to define a section of $p$, and join the identity to the section by a straight-line homotopy of simplex coordinates.
proofs.scope: The member of the family for numerable open covers, due to Segal. The homotopy colimit is the realization of the Čech nerve; the form for filtered spaces is the record higher homotopy van Kampen theorem.

roles.why: The sets $U_\lambda$ define the Čech diagram, and each point $x$ lies in the sets $U_\lambda$ with $\lambda \in \Lambda_x$.
The partition of unity gives the section $s$ and the target of the straight-line homotopy.

steps.slogan: Describe the points of the homotopy colimit $E$ by a point and simplex coordinates.
steps.detail: Let $\Lambda_x = \{\lambda : x \in U_\lambda\}$. A point of $E$ is a pair $(x, t)$ where $x \in X$ and $t$ is a probability vector with finite support in $\Lambda_x$. The projection is $p(x, t) = x$. The topology is that of the [geometric realization](c:geometric-realization) of the Čech nerve.

steps.slogan: Define the section $s(x) = (x, (\varphi_\lambda(x))_\lambda)$ from the partition of unity.
steps.detail: If $\varphi_\lambda(x) > 0$ then $x \in U_\lambda$, so $(\varphi_\lambda(x))$ is supported in $\Lambda_x$ and $s(x) \in E$. Local finiteness means that near each point only finitely many coordinates are nonzero, which gives continuity of $s$. Clearly $p \circ s = \mathrm{id}_X$.

steps.slogan: Join $\mathrm{id}_E$ to $s \circ p$ by moving the simplex coordinates in a straight line.
steps.detail: Put $H_\tau(x, t) = (x, (1 - \tau)\, t + \tau\, \varphi(x))$. Both $t$ and $\varphi(x)$ are supported in $\Lambda_x$, so $H_\tau$ is defined, and continuity again follows from local finiteness. We get $H_0 = \mathrm{id}_E$ and $H_1 = s \circ p$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $p$ is a homotopy equivalence with homotopy inverse $s$.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 3 give $p \circ s = \mathrm{id}_X$ and $s \circ p \simeq \mathrm{id}_E$. So $p$ is a [homotopy equivalence](c:homotopy-equivalence), and the homotopy type of $X$ is the homotopy type of the homotopy colimit of the Čech diagram of the pieces.

concepts.c:open-cover: The cover supplies the pieces whose homotopy colimit is built.
concepts.c:homotopy-colimit: The homotopy colimit of the Čech diagram is the space that maps to $X$.
concepts.c:homotopy-equivalence: The section and the straight-line homotopy make $p$ a homotopy equivalence.
concepts.c:geometric-realization: The homotopy colimit is the geometric realization of the Čech nerve.

source.note: Segal's proof of Proposition 4.1 in G. Segal, Classifying spaces and spectral sequences, Publications Mathématiques de l'IHÉS 34 (1968), 105-112.
